encyclopedia.definition: An EPIRB is a vessel-registered emergency transmitter designed to broadcast distress signals on 406 MHz to rescue authorities via the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system.
encyclopedia.content:
An Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) is a core safety component of the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS). Unlike a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB), which is registered to an individual, an EPIRB is officially coded to a specific vessel using its Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) or serial number.

Upon deployment, the beacon transmits a 406 MHz distress alert to Cospas-Sarsat satellites alongside a low-power 121.5 MHz homing signal for local search vessels. Understanding [how GPS works](/en/blog/what-to-buy-for-a-sailor-25-yachting-gift-ideas/) demonstrates how GNSS-enabled EPIRBs shrink the search radius from 5 kilometers (2.7 nautical miles) down to within 100 meters (328 feet).

EPIRBs fall into two operational categories. Category 1 utilizes a Hydrostatic Release Unit (HRU) that automatically frees and activates the beacon when submerged to a depth between 1.5 and 4 meters (4.9 to 13.1 feet). Category 2 requires manual release. International standards specify a minimum battery operating life of 48 hours at -20°C (-4°F). When sourcing safety [yacht equipment](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/), skippers must rigorously monitor HRU expiration dates (typically 2 years) and battery service intervals (5–10 years). The swift loss of vessels like the superyacht Bayesian emphasizes the life-saving role of accessible distress beacons during sudden sinkings.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Differentiate EPIRB (vessel-bound beacon) from individual PLBs or aviation ELTs. Never mount Category 1 float-free brackets under overhangs or biminis that block ascent.

encyclopedia.definition: A resilient bumper device (typically air-filled PVC, polyurethane elastomer, or foam) deployed along a vessel's hull to absorb kinetic energy and prevent damage during mooring or ship-to-ship berthing.
encyclopedia.content:
A marine fender is a dedicated damping device designed to absorb the kinetic energy of a vessel during berthing against docks, piers, or other boats. To distinguish this homonym, in nautical contexts a fender refers strictly to protective boat bumpers, not automotive mudguards or musical equipment. Modern leisure craft fenders are typically manufactured from soft PVC, polyurethane elastomers, or closed-cell foam.

According to Wikipedia, fenders function as elastic buffer systems engineered to combine high energy absorption with low reaction force. Proper sizing depends on displacement and length: a common standard is 2.5 cm (1 in) of fender diameter for every 1.5 m (5 ft) of boat length. For a typical 12-meter sailboat, a minimum of 4 to 6 cylindrical fenders per side plus one large spherical roving fender is recommended. Inflatable models require a precise working internal pressure between 0.15 bar and 0.20 bar (2.1 to 2.9 psi); over-inflation reduces shock-absorption capacity and hazards structural failure under heavy load.

When approaching a busy [yacht marina](/en/blog/what-is-a-yacht-marina-port-vs-marina-for-yachts-explained-2/), fenders are suspended at the vessel's widest beam using clove hitch knots secured to stanchions or toe rails. Extra precautions are critical when squalls or a squally [catabatic wind](/en/blog/what-is-a-catabatic-wind-and-how-is-it-dangerous-for-boaters/) threaten to push the vessel heavily against the quay wall.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Do not over-inflate air fenders beyond 0.2 bar. Secure fender lanyards with a clove hitch to stanchions or toe rails, and keep fender surfaces free of salt crystals and grit to protect gelcoat.

encyclopedia.definition: Freeboard is the vertical distance measured from the waterline to the upper deck level at the lowest point where water can enter the vessel.
encyclopedia.content:
Freeboard is a critical measurement in yacht design, defined as the distance from the waterline to the deck at the point of least height, typically amidships, where water could otherwise ingress. According to the IMO Load Lines Convention, for commercial vessels, freeboard is measured relative to the ship's load line, ensuring a minimum reserve buoyancy. In yachts, freeboard directly affects safety, performance, and interior volume.

A low freeboard reduces weight and aerodynamic drag, enhancing speed — common on racing yachts. However, it increases the risk of swamping in rough seas. The incident of the yacht Polbream, which sailed 150 miles without a keel, illustrates how quickly a vessel's freeboard can be compromised; losing the keel caused the boat to settle lower, reducing its freeboard and stability. (Read more about this [unexpected adventure](/en/blog/7-luchshih-podarkov-dlya-yahtsmena-v-2025-godu/)). Conversely, a high freeboard provides greater interior cabin space and better wave protection, as seen in ocean cruisers. It also contributes to meeting stability regulations by increasing reserve buoyancy.

When choosing a yacht, consider the trade-offs: a higher freeboard offers comfort and safety, while a lower freeboard may improve sailing performance. For further insights into yacht design, explore our [yacht design tag](/en/tags/yacht-design/).

Practically, owners should monitor freeboard changes: excessive loading reduces freeboard, compromising safety. Always adhere to the manufacturer's maximum load recommendations.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Freeboard should not be confused with 'draft' (the depth below the waterline). While draft measures how deep the hull extends, freeboard measures the height above the water. On planing powerboats, static freeboard may differ significantly from running freeboard due to dynamic lift.

encyclopedia.seoDescription: Freeboard is the distance from waterline to deck, crucial for safety and performance. Learn how it affects yacht design and stability.

encyclopedia.definition: A genoa sail is a large overlapping headsail whose clew extends aft past the mast line.
encyclopedia.content:
A genoa sail (often simply called a genoa) is a large headsail whose clew extends aft past the mast, overlapping the mainsail. According to Wikipedia, this overlapping headsail increases a vessel's sail area and speed in light to moderate winds. Geometrically, a genoa is distinguished from a working jib by its Luff Perpendicular (LP) measurement: while a working jib has an LP of 100% or less relative to the foretriangle base (J), a genoa typically ranges from 130% to 150% LP (commonly categorized as a Genoa #1 at ~150% or Genoa #2 at ~135%).

Nautical terminology distinguishes the genoa sail from the port city of Genoa in Italy, as well as from the "genoa car" (or lead car), which slides along the deck track to adjust the sheet angle.

On the water, trimming a genoa requires precision. During basic maneuvers like [tacking](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/), the overlapping canvas must clear the mast and shrouds before being hauled in on the new leeward side. Managing the heavy sheet loads requires efficient [yacht rope handling with winches and blocks](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/). In winds exceeding 15–18 knots, sailors roll up (furl) or replace the genoa with a smaller working jib to maintain vessel stability and control.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Used mainly on close-hauled to beam reach courses in light to moderate winds. Requires adjusting lead cars for proper sheet lead.

encyclopedia.definition: A satellite-based radionavigation system providing precise geographic coordinates, speed over ground, and course over ground for vessels worldwide.
encyclopedia.content:
In maritime navigation, GPS (Global Positioning System) refers to the space-based radionavigation system operated by the United States Space Force. Outside nautical terminology, the acronym GPS may denote non-maritime organizations such as the Great Public Schools Association of Queensland, but for mariners, it is the primary electronic positioning standard.

The system calculates a vessel's position by measuring the time delay of radio signals transmitted from a constellation of Earth-orbiting satellites. A minimum of 4 satellite signals is required to compute latitude, longitude, and precise clock bias. Standard marine receivers offer a horizontal accuracy of 2 to 5 meters, which can be improved to sub-meter precision (<1 meter) using Satellite-Based Augmentation Systems (SBAS) or Differential GPS (DGPS).

Integrated into modern marine networks via NMEA protocols, the receiver continuously calculates Course Over Ground (COG, measured in true degrees from 000° to 359°) and Speed Over Ground (SOG, expressed in knots, where 1 knot equals 1.852 km/h). Understanding [how GPS functions in electronic navigation](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/) is essential for skipper decision-making, as COG and SOG represent the true movement across the seabed including current and leeway effects. However, electronic positioning should never fully replace traditional seamanship. Relying solely on satellites exposes the vessel to risks like signal jamming or power failures, making the proper use of [the marine compass](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/) an indispensable backup for safe navigation.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Used for electronic charting, waypoint navigation, anchor watch alarms, and AIS integration. Always maintain paper chart plotting or magnetic compass verification as fail-safes.

encyclopedia.definition: A gybe (also spelled jibe) is a sailing maneuver in which the stern of a vessel passes through the wind line, shifting the mainsail and boom from one side of the boat to the other while sailing downwind.
encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia reference material, the term *gybe* (alternatively spelled *jibe*) denotes a sailing maneuver in which the stern of a vessel crosses the wind line, transferring the mainboom and mainsail from one side to the other while sailing downwind. Unlike tacking, where the bow turns through the wind, a gybe is performed on off-wind points of sail such as broad reach or running downwind.

In practical seamanship, executing a gybe requires clear communication and precise crew coordination. The primary danger of downwind turns is an uncontrolled gybe caused by a sudden wind shift or steering error, which can cause violent boom movement across the cockpit, posing severe injury risks to crew and structural damage to the rig. To ensure a safe maneuver, the crew hauls the mainsheet in tightly toward the centerline before the helm rotates the stern through the wind. Once the mainsail flips across, the mainsheet is smoothly eased out on the new tack.

When mastering [essential sailing maneuvers for beginners](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/), sailors also learn to avoid hazardous variations like a "Chinese gybe," where the upper section of the mainsail gybes before the lower part due to insufficient boom vang tension. Understanding how a sail generates aerodynamic forces, as detailed in our guide on [how a sail works on a yacht](/en/blog/how-a-sail-works-on-a-yacht-classic-and-modern-explanation/), aids in controlling sail pressure during these downwind transitions. Additionally, nautical terminology distinguishes the gybe maneuver from non-maritime homonyms such as the acronym GY!BE (Godspeed You! Black Emperor).
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Spelling varies by region: 'gybe' is preferred in British and Commonwealth English, whereas 'jibe' is standard in American English. Always check for a rigged boom preventer before initiating a planned gybe.

encyclopedia.definition: A line of running rigging used to hoist a sail, yard, flag, or ladder up a mast or stay.
encyclopedia.content:
A halyard is a primary running rigging line used to hoist a sail, yard, flag, or ladder up a mast or stay. Unlike sheets, which control a sail's angle to the wind, a halyard exerts vertical tension along the luff. As noted in Wikipedia's historical definition, the term originates from the Middle English halier ("a rope to haul with") combined with yard (the spar at the head of a square sail).

On modern cruising yachts ranging from 30 to 50 feet (9–15 meters) in length, halyards typically measure between 8 and 12 mm in diameter. Mainsail and headsail halyards require low-stretch synthetic cores, such as UHMWPE/Dyneema wrapped in a polyester jacket, capable of withstanding working loads of 2,000 to 6,000 kgf without creeping. Proper [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/) involves running halyards through deck organizers, securing them in rope clutches, and tensioning them on winches. Mastering these lines is essential for understanding [yachting terminology](/en/blog/yachting-terminology-for-dummies-77-words-you-need-to-know-before-traveling-on-a-yacht/).

Halyards are categorized by function: mainsail halyard, jib/genoa halyard, and spinnaker halyard. In practical sail trimming, tension directly affects draft position: insufficient halyard tension allows the draft to drift aft, reducing upwind efficiency, while over-tensioning produces vertical wrinkles along the luff.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Do not confuse halyards (hoist sails vertically) with sheets (adjust sail angle to wind). Always engage the rope clutch before easing a halyard off the winch drum.

encyclopedia.definition: Heading is the direction in which the longitudinal axis (bow) of a vessel is pointed at any given moment, measured in degrees from 000° to 359° clockwise from North.
encyclopedia.content:
Heading defines the instantaneous orientation of a vessel's longitudinal axis relative to North, expressed in degrees from 000° to 359°. In marine navigation, it is crucial to distinguish heading from Course Over Ground (COG). While heading indicates where the boat's bow is pointing, COG represents the actual track of the vessel across the seabed, influenced by current, tidal streams, and leeway caused by wind.

Heading can be expressed relative to three different references: True North (True Heading), Magnetic North (Magnetic Heading), and Compass North (Compass Heading). True Heading aligns with geographic meridians. Magnetic Heading accounts for magnetic variation (the angular difference between true and magnetic norths), while Compass Heading incorporates both variation and local magnetic interference on board, known as deviation. Navigators must systematically apply variation and deviation corrections when converting between these values.

While modern satellite receivers determine COG, an onboard magnetic or electronic compass is essential to measure true heading. Understanding this difference is vital when navigating challenging regions, such as when planning [yachting in Corsica](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/). As referenced in navigation standards documented on Wikipedia, differentiating between heading and course over ground is essential for collision avoidance under COLREGs and for calculating drift corrections. Proper mastery of [marine compass operation](/en/blog/yachting-in-corsica-the-best-routes-locations-and-vacation-secrets/) ensures accurate dead reckoning and safe vessel control in all conditions.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Do not confuse Heading (orientation of the vessel's bow) with COG (actual track over the seabed) or Bearing (direction to a target object). Always convert between Compass, Magnetic, and True headings by applying deviation and variation.

encyclopedia.definition: A seamanship maneuver where sails and rudder are set in opposition to bring a sailing vessel to a relative stop and controlled drift.
encyclopedia.content:
As defined in Wikipedia, heaving to is a method of slowing a sailing vessel's forward progress and locking the helm and sails so that constant steering is not required. Executed by tacking without backing the jib (leaving it backed to windward), easing the mainsail, and locking the helm hard to windward, the technique balances opposing aerodynamic forces. The backed jib pushes the bow away from the wind, while the turned rudder forces it back up, causing the yacht to settle into a stable drift at a speed of 1 to 2 knots at an angle of roughly 45° to 60° to the true wind.

A key hydrodynamic benefit is the creation of a smooth wake or slick to windward, which breaks the energy of cresting seas before they strike the hull. This makes heaving to an indispensable storm strategy and a practical rest tactic for singlehanded or shorthanded crews needing to take a meal, attend to gear, or reef sails. Modern navigation tools help monitor this drift movement; learn more about tracking position in our article on [how GPS works in sailing](/en/blog/sailing-superstitions-from-neptune-to-the-ban-on-bananas-on-board/). Under COLREGs, a vessel hove to remains on its active tack (preferably starboard tack to retain stand-on status), distinguishing it from a power-driven vessel ordered to stop by law enforcement or a unrigged vessel lying to.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Essential heavy-weather tactic and short-handed sailing maneuver. Prefer starboard tack when hove to under COLREGs.

encyclopedia.definition: The watertight structural shell of a vessel that provides buoyancy, stability, and structural integrity under hydrodynamic and aerodynamic loads.
encyclopedia.content:
A hull is the watertight body of a ship or sailboat that provides buoyancy, housing for the crew, and structural support for rigging and machinery. In nautical terminology, a vessel’s hull must be distinguished from homonyms such as the outer husk of a seed or the verb meaning to remove husks. The principal exact dimensions defining a hull include Length Overall (LOA, total length from stem to stern), Length Waterline (LWL, length of the hull submerged in water), Beam (maximum width of the hull), and Draft (vertical distance from the waterline to the deepest part of the keel or hull).

Hull designs generally fall into displacement and planing categories. Displacement hulls remain submerged and push through water, whereas planing hulls generate hydrodynamic lift at higher speeds. Internal framing consisting of floors, frames, and stringers supports the outer skin, constructed from modern GRP (glass-reinforced plastic), aluminum, or steel. As noted in Wikipedia’s documentation on the *Iron-hulled sailing ship*, the historical shift from timber to iron and steel hulls dramatically enhanced structural longevity and cargo capacity.

Maintaining structural integrity is critical for seamanship. In extreme [incidents involving keel loss](/en/blog/150-miles-without-a-keel-polbream-s-unexpected-adventure/), a resilient hull can preserve reserve buoyancy and prevent immediate capsizing. On modern cruisers with [twin steering wheels](/en/blog/why-are-there-two-helms-on-a-yacht-a-detailed-guide-for-beginners/), wide-beam hulls optimize interior volume while maintaining control under heel.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Refers specifically to the watertight shell of the vessel. Do not confuse with superstructure, deck fittings, or rig components.

encyclopedia.definition: A triangular headsail set forward of the mast along the forestay, providing primary aerodynamic drive and steering balance.
encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia, a jib is a triangular sail that sets ahead of the foremast of a sailing vessel, with its forward corner (tack) fixed to the bowsprit, bow, or deck. On modern bermudan-rigged sloops, the term "jib" specifically refers to a headsail whose clew does not overlap the mast significantly, or remains entirely within the foretriangle.

Sailmakers classify headsails using the Luff Perpendicular (LP) measurement—the perpendicular line drawn from the clew to the luff. A standard working jib typically has an LP of 100% or less of the J-dimension (the foredeck distance from the mast to the forestay). In contrast, a genoa features a larger LP ranging between 110% and 150%, overlapping the mainsail considerably. On cutter-rigged vessels with multiple headsails, the forward-most sail is the jib (or flying jib), while the inner sail is the staysail.

In practical sailing, the jib creates a high-velocity airflow slot between itself and the mainsail, dramatically increasing lift on upwind points of sail. Efficient crew coordination requires proper [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/) to adjust jib sheets and fairlead tracks. During maneuvers such as [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/), releasing and backing the jib sheet at the correct instant ensures smooth turns. Note that in non-maritime contexts, "jib" refers to the operating arm of a mechanical crane or a camera boom.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Used for headsails with LP <= 100%. Do not confuse with the mechanical jib arm of a crane or camera rig.

encyclopedia.definition: The central longitudinal structural element at the bottom of a hull, or a weighted underwater fin that provides stability and resists lateral leeway on modern sailing vessels.
encyclopedia.content:
In ship construction, according to Wikipedia, the keel is the bottom-most longitudinal structural element of a watercraft, traditionally serving as the primary backbone of the hull. In modern sailing yacht design, a clear distinction must be drawn between this internal structural keel and the external fin keel (or ballast keel). While the backbone is integrated into the hull structure, the ballast keel is an external hydrodynamic appendage bolted to the underside of the vessel.

The keel serves two primary practical functions: generating hydrodynamic lift to counteract lateral drift (leeway) when sailing close-hauled and creating a righting moment to resist heeling forces exerted by the wind. Ballast—typically cast iron or lead—is concentrated inside the fin or lower bulb. On standard cruising yachts, ballast comprises 30% to 45% of total vessel displacement, providing positive stability at significant heel angles. Modern keel drafts typically range from 1.5 meters for shallow-draft wing designs to over 2.5 meters for high-performance deep fins.

A failure or loss of the ballast keel severely compromises stability and leads to an immediate capsize risk under sail, as highlighted in the infamous [Polbream incident](/en/blog/150-miles-without-a-keel-polbream-s-unexpected-adventure/). Homonymically, the nautical keel must be distinguished from the anatomical keel (sternum ridge) in birds or the historical English unit of coal weight (approx. 21.2 metric tons). Maintaining keel integrity requires regular inspection of keel bolts and structural floor grids, especially after accidental groundings. For captains managing safety systems onboard, finding practical tools and gear can be explored in our guide to [top gifts for yachtsmen](/en/blog/the-7-best-gifts-for-the-yachtsman-in-2025/).
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Inspect the bilge area around keel washers after grounding to verify there is no delamination or water ingress.

encyclopedia.definition: A nautical unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour (exactly 1.852 km/h or approximately 0.514 m/s).
encyclopedia.content:
A knot (abbreviated as kn or kt) is a non-SI unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour, defined precisely as 1.852 kilometers per hour (approximately 0.514 meters per second).

It is essential to distinguish the homonym: a knot as a measure of velocity versus a knot tied in a line (such as a bowline or clove hitch). The speed unit historically derives from counting knots tied at regular intervals on a log line cast overboard to determine a vessel's speed through the water.

In modern seamanship, navigators monitor two distinct speed parameters expressed in knots: Speed Through Water (STW), measured by a paddlewheel log, and Speed Over Ground (SOG), derived from satellite positioning systems. Integrating data from [GPS and electronic navigation](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/) allows the skipper to account for set and drift caused by currents and leeway. Comparing these speed vector metrics alongside headings from a [marine compass](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/) is fundamental for dead reckoning. According to Wikipedia's entry on speed sailing, officially recording maximum craft velocities requires strict measurement protocols managed by governing bodies like the WSSRC.

Calculating navigation distance is straightforward with knots: traveling at 6 knots for 2 hours yields exactly 12 nautical miles.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Never say 'knots per hour' when referring to speed, as a knot is already a rate of nautical miles per hour. Always distinguish from line knots used in rigging.
encyclopedia.seoTitle: Knot (Speed Unit): Marine Navigation Definition

encyclopedia.definition: A sea mark used in the IALA Maritime Buoyage System to indicate the port or starboard edge of a channel relative to the direction of buoyage.
encyclopedia.content: A lateral mark is a buoy or fixed beacon that defines the boundary of a navigable channel. According to the IALA (International Association of Marine Aids to Navigation and Lighthouse Authorities) system, these marks tell a mariner which side to leave them on when following the conventional direction of buoyage – usually upstream in rivers or into a harbour from seaward. The world is divided into two regions: IALA Region A (Europe, Africa, most of Asia) and Region B (the Americas, Japan, Philippines). In Region A, red cylindrical port marks are left to port (left) when entering a harbour, while green conical starboard marks are left to starboard. In Region B the colours are reversed. Knowing your region is essential; mistaking a port mark for a starboard mark can ground a vessel. A traditional way to verify your position relative to a mark is to take a compass bearing and cross-check with the chart – a technique thoroughly covered in our article on [how to use a marine compass](/en/blog/gps-ais-i-radar-tri-glaza-vashey-yahty-znaete-li-vy-v-chyom-raznitsa/). For a broader view of all navigation aids, including electronic systems that complement lateral marks, explore the [Navigation](/en/tags/navigation/) tag.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Before entering a port, identify the local IALA region and confirm the direction of buoyage from the chart. In Region A, remember 'red left returning' (i.e. keep red marks to port when coming from sea). Always cross-check visually with the chart and use a compass bearing to avoid confusion.

encyclopedia.definition: Geographical latitude is the angular distance of a location north or south of the Earth's equator, expressed in degrees from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles.
encyclopedia.content:
Latitude (geographical latitude) is the angular distance of a point north or south of the Earth's equator, measured along a meridian. It ranges from 0° at the equator to 90° N (+90°) at the North Pole and 90° S (-90°) at the South Pole. In maritime navigation, geographical latitude must be distinguished from astronomical latitude (which accounts for local gravity anomalies) and ecliptic celestial latitude used in astronomy.

In practical seamanship, latitude provides the foundational scale for measuring distances on nautical charts. By definition, one minute of latitude (1′) equals exactly one nautical mile, which is standardized as 1,852 meters (approx. 6,076 feet). One degree of latitude (1°) comprises 60 minutes and equals 60 nautical miles. Consequently, navigators always use the vertical latitude scale on the side margins of a Mercator projection chart to measure distances with dividers.

Modern receivers ensure precise positioning where [GPS on a sailboat](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/) displays latitude in degrees, minutes, and decimal minutes (e.g., 43°30.50′ N). Determining latitude celestial-wise has ancient roots. According to Wikipedia, Arab navigators of the late 9th century invented the kamal—a simple wooden celestial navigation tool—to determine latitude by observing stars, marking the earliest quantitative navigation method.

While a traditional [marine compass on board](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/) provides direction, accurate position plotting requires entering latitude correctly into passage plans. Understanding latitude measurements ensures skippers correctly interpret chart scales and avoid critical errors in route calculation.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Latitude is always stated before longitude in position reporting. Use only the vertical latitude scale on Mercator charts to measure nautical miles.

encyclopedia.definition: The aft (trailing) edge of a triangular sail, running between the head and the clew.
encyclopedia.content: The leech is the aft edge of a triangular sail, connecting the head at the top of the mast to the clew at the end of the boom. Unlike the luff, the leech is not attached to any spar and is free to fly, often with a slight curve known as "roach." This roach is not a flaw but a crucial aerodynamic feature that adds sail area and improves efficiency, particularly when sailing upwind. Proper leech tension is a fundamental aspect of [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/rabota-s-verevkami-na-yahte-lebedki-i-bloki-dlya-chaynikov/), as it directly dictates the sail's shape and power. A leech that is too open will spill wind, depowering the sail, while a leech that is too closed, or "hooked," creates excessive drag and heeling. Control is achieved primarily through the mainsheet and boom vang. It is important to distinguish the mainsail leech from the leech of a jib, which is also called the leech but is adjusted using jib sheet fairleads. According to Wikipedia, the term is derived from the Old English word for the edge of a cloth. To master leech control in real conditions, it's essential to practice [essential sailing maneuvers](/en/blog/osnovnye-parusnye-manevry-dlya-novichkov-overshtag-i-fordevind-prostymi-slovami/) like tacking, where easing and trimming the leech correctly ensures a smooth and efficient turn through the wind.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: The term applies to both mainsails and headsails. In the context of the mainsail, sailors often refer to "tightening the leech" to increase its tension and power.

encyclopedia.definition: The direction downwind from a reference point, or the side of a vessel sheltered from the wind.
encyclopedia.content:
The term "leeward" (pronounced LEW-erd or LEE-wərd) describes the direction downwind from a given point of reference. As defined in Wikipedia, leeward is the side or direction towards which the wind is blowing, serving as the opposite of windward.

In seamanship, a clear distinction must be made between the leeward side of a vessel and a leeward shore (commonly called a lee shore). A yacht’s leeward side (or lee side) is the side opposite to where the wind originates; as the boat heels under sail, this becomes the lower side. Conversely, a leeward shore is land positioned downwind of the boat. While the lee side of a hull offers shelter from wind and spray, a lee shore presents a grave hazard to navigation because wind and sea state continuously drive the vessel toward shallow water or rocks.

Leeward positioning also governs right-of-way under Rule 12 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs). When two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the vessel which is to windward must keep out of the way of the vessel which is to leeward.

Executing basic maneuvers such as [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/) requires smooth control of sails as they swing across the leeward side. To counter leeway—the sideways drift toward leeward caused by wind pressure—modern hulls rely heavily on effective [sailboat keels](/en/blog/types-of-sailboat-keels-how-to-choose-the-right-one/) to provide hydrodynamic lift and directional stability.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Do not confuse the leeward side of a vessel (sheltered side) with a leeward shore (a dangerous shoreline located downwind of the vessel).

encyclopedia.definition: A personal flotation device designed to keep an unconscious person's head above water with airway clear.
encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia, a personal flotation device (PFD) is a vest or suit designed to keep a user afloat in water. In marine practice, a strict technical distinction is made between a buoyancy aid (50N) and a true life jacket (100N, 150N, or 275N standards under ISO 12402). A 50 Newton buoyancy aid assists conscious swimmers in sheltered waters, but lacks the turning force to keep an incapacitated wearer's head clear of waves.

For offshore and coastal cruising, a 150 Newton (150N) gas-inflatable life jacket serves as the standard safety equipment. When inflated, it provides sufficient positive buoyancy to automatically turn an unconscious person face-up within 5 seconds, maintaining the airways at least 80–120 mm above the water level. For severe ocean passage-making with heavy foul-weather gear, 275 Newton jackets are deployed to overcome trapped air inside oilskins. Automatic models utilize hydrostatic (Hammar) or water-soluble pill triggers, alongside manual pull cords and oral inflation tubes.

Understanding essential safety gear is a core element of basic [yachting terminology](/en/blog/what-to-buy-for-a-sailor-25-yachting-gift-ideas/). Personal life jackets often rank high among practical [yachting gifts](/en/blog/yachting-terminology-for-dummies-77-words-you-need-to-know-before-traveling-on-a-yacht/) for crew members. Every offshore jacket must feature a crotch strap, whistle, reflective tape, and a safety harness attachment point (D-ring) rated to ISO 12401 standards.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Inspect CO2 cylinder tightness and arming status before every passage. Always secure the crotch strap to prevent the jacket from riding up.

encyclopedia.definition: A self-inflating collective lifesaving appliance designed to keep survivors afloat and protected from exposure after abandoning a vessel.
encyclopedia.content:
A life raft is an essential collective lifesaving appliance engineered to preserve human life when abandoning a vessel during catastrophic hull compromise, fire, or sinking. Unlike a standard inflatable tender or open lifeboat, a marine life raft is packed under pressure inside a rigid fiberglass canister or weather-resistant valise. It features a self-deploying high-visibility canopy, dual independent buoyancy chambers, an insulated floor to mitigate hypothermia, and weighted water ballast pockets (typically 200 to 400 liters total capacity) beneath the hull to prevent capsizing in severe wave action.

Inflation is triggered automatically when the painter line (usually 15 meters or longer) is pulled, activating a high-pressure compressed gas cylinder containing a carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrogen (N2) mixture. Modern life rafts adhere to ISO 9650-1 (offshore) or ISO 9650-2 (coastal) standards, or SOLAS requirements for commercial and oceanic voyages, incorporating emergency survival packs (Pack A or Pack B) containing distress flares, drinking water, and first-aid kits. A hydrostatic release unit (HRU) allows the raft to float free and inflate automatically if the vessel sinks to a depth of 1.5 to 4.0 meters. Proper skipper training, certified via recognized [skipper certificates](/en/blog/what-to-buy-for-a-sailor-25-yachting-gift-ideas/), ensures correct mounting and emergency deployment procedures. Including essential items like EPIRBs alongside standard [yacht equipment kits](/en/blog/types-of-yachting-licences-and-skippers-certificates-how-to-become-a-captain-and-charter-a-yacht-anywhere-in-the-world/) greatly increases the probability of rapid search-and-rescue response. Mandatory inspection and recertification must occur every 1 to 3 years at licensed service stations.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Ensure the painter line is securely tied to a strong point (cleat or strongback) before launching. Verify that the Hydrostatic Release Unit (HRU) is within its valid service period.

encyclopedia.definition: Geographic longitude is the angular distance measured east or west from the Prime Meridian (Greenwich) to the meridian of a given point, ranging from 0° to 180° E or W.
encyclopedia.content:
Geographic longitude specifies the east-west position of a vessel on the Earth's surface. It is measured in degrees (°), arcminutes ('), and arcseconds (''), or decimal minutes, ranging from 0° at the Prime Meridian in Greenwich to 180° East (E) or West (W). Unlike latitude lines, meridians of longitude converge at the poles. Therefore, while one minute of latitude consistently equals one nautical mile (1852 meters), the physical distance of one degree of longitude varies from 60 nautical miles at the equator to zero at the geographic poles, calculated as 60 nautical miles multiplied by the cosine of the latitude.

Longitude is directly linked to time: because the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, 15° of longitude corresponds to a one-hour shift in local solar time (1° per 4 minutes). Determining longitude at sea was historically a major navigation challenge until John Harrison developed the marine chronometer, a breakthrough chronicled in Dava Sobel’s historical account *Longitude*.

In modern sailing, understanding [how GPS works and the role of electronic navigation](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/) explains how receivers instantly calculate longitude alongside latitude. Mariners must distinguish geographic longitude from celestial or ecliptic longitude used in astronomy, as well as the book title. Reliable dead reckoning requires combining modern chartplotter coordinates with a traditional [compass on a sailboat](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/) to cross-check headings and positioning.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: When recording coordinates in a logbook, longitude is always written with three digits for degrees (e.g., 008°15.4' W or 124°02.1' E) to prevent confusion with latitude values.

encyclopedia.definition: The leading edge of a sail, extending from head to tack, and the action of turning the bow of a sailboat into the wind.
encyclopedia.content: The luff is the forward edge of a sail, running from the head to the tack. In Bermuda-rigged boats it is often attached to the mast via slides or a bolt rope. The term ‘luff’ also describes the maneuver of steering the bow into the wind, causing the sail to flutter. Distinguishing between the physical edge and the maneuver is fundamental. Luff tension is a primary sail trim control: it determines the draft position and overall shape. Tension is adjusted with the halyard and, for finer control, a cunningham downhaul, which leads through a cringle in the luff just above the tack. According to Wikipedia, Briggs Cunningham invented this gear for swift racing adjustments. Increasing luff tension pulls the draft forward and flattens the sail—ideal for strong winds; easing it moves draft aft for light air. Watching the telltales along the luff helps the crew detect optimal trim and avoid flow separation. Understanding how the luff interacts with airflow is crucial; our article on [how a sail works](/en/blog/osnovnye-parusnye-manevry-dlya-novichkov-overshtag-i-fordevind-prostymi-slovami/) explains the aerodynamics, and mastering [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/kak-rabotaet-parus-na-yahte-klassicheskoe-i-sovremennoe-ob-yasnenie/) helps avoid unintentional luffing. Proper luff control ensures efficient, safe sailing.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: In casual sailing speech, ‘luff’ may refer to the sail edge or the act of luffing. Context clarifies meaning. Specify ‘luff of the sail’ for the edge and ‘luff up’ for the maneuver.

encyclopedia.definition: A self-contained navigation instrument that utilizes Earth's magnetic field to indicate vessel heading and bearings.
encyclopedia.content:
According to historical details from Wikipedia's article "History of the compass", the device evolved over two millennia from early Chinese lodestones to liquid-filled marine instruments introduced in the early 20th century. On a modern yacht, the magnetic compass remains the primary non-electronic instrument for directional orientation.

It is essential to distinguish the magnetic compass from a gyrocompass or a standard hiking compass. Unlike electronic sensors, a magnetic compass responds directly to the Earth's magnetic field, indicating magnetic north rather than true geographic north. The angular difference between true north and magnetic north is termed magnetic variation (Var), measured in degrees East or West. Additionally, magnetic interference from onboard equipment causes compass deviation (Dev). To obtain the true heading (TH) from the compass heading (CH), navigators apply the formula: TH = CH + (±Var) + (±Dev).

A standard marine compass features a card graduated from 0° to 360°, submerged in a damping liquid within a compass bowl, and mounted on gimbals to withstand vessel heel and pitch. Knowing [how to use a marine compass](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/) is critical when preparing passage plans alongside [accurate weather forecasts](/en/blog/weather-forecast-sites-your-guide-to-the-most-accurate-marine-weather-websites-for-sea-and-sailing/). Even in an era dominated by GPS, the magnetic compass provides an unshakeable backup that requires zero electrical power.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Always account for local magnetic variation and vessel deviation when converting compass headings to true courses.

encyclopedia.definition: A mainsail is the primary sail rigged on and behind the main mast of a fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel.
encyclopedia.content:
The mainsail is the primary sail set behind the mainmast on modern bermudan-rigged sailboats. While historically the largest sail aboard, modern high-aspect sloops often feature a mainsail smaller than their headsails. In nautical terminology, the term mainsail refers strictly to the main propulsion sail on the main mast and should not be confused with secondary foresails or storm sails like the trysail. According to Wikipedia, a mainsail is the sail rigged aft of the main mast on a fore-and-aft rigged vessel, with its foot normally attached to a boom.

Rigging and controlling the mainsail relies on key elements of running rigging. The luff attaches along the mast track or furling slot, the foot secures to the boom, and the clew connects to the outhaul. Halyards raise the sail, while control lines like the mainsheet and boom vang govern its angle and tension. Efficient sail control requires proficient [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/), where winches provide necessary mechanical advantage to manage high loads on the mainsheet and halyard.

During tactical sailing, trimming the mainsail dictates boat balance and steering characteristics. Precise mainsail adjustment is crucial when carrying out fundamental maneuvers such as [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/), where controlled boom sweeps prevent accidental gybes. In extreme weather exceeding 30 knots of wind, reefing reduces mainsail surface area in pre-measured stages to maintain stability before swapping to a heavy-weather trysail.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Always distinguish the mainsail from headsails (genoa, jib). Trimming involves halyard tension, mainsheet lead, outhaul, and boom vang controls. Reef the mainsail early as wind increases.

encyclopedia.definition: An emergency situation where a crew member or passenger falls off a vessel into the water, as well as the standard emergency shout and recovery maneuver.
encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia, 'Man overboard!' is the traditional emergency exclamation given aboard a vessel to indicate that a crew member or passenger has fallen into the water. In modern seamanship, the acronym MOB refers both to the verbal alarm call and the tactical sequence executed to locate and retrieve the victim. Upon sighting a casualty, the observer must shout the alarm, maintain continuous physical pointing at the person, launch a lifebuoy with a drogue, and instantly press the MOB button on the helm chartplotter. This action saves the precise GPS coordinates (WGS-84) to assist tactical maneuvering. Understanding [how GPS works](/en/blog/sailing-superstitions-from-neptune-to-the-ban-on-bananas-on-board/) and pairing it with personal AIS beacons significantly increases rescue probability in rough seas.

Recovery maneuvers vary by propulsion type and sea state. Sailing vessels usually perform a Quick Stop or Figure Eight maneuver to keep the yacht within a 50–100 meter radius of the casualty. Power vessels in open waters often execute the Williamson turn—turning hard toward the fallen side until 60 degrees off course, then hard over opposite—to align with the original track line. Time is critical: at a water temperature of 10°C (50°F), hypothermia and loss of consciousness can occur in 30 to 60 minutes. While ancient [sailing superstitions](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/) viewed falling overboard as a fateful omen, contemporary safety relies on safety harnesses, jacklines, and drilled recovery maneuvers.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Distinguish between MOB as an emergency call ('Man overboard!'), the situational event, and the dedicated MOB waypoint button on chartplotters.

encyclopedia.definition: An active radio detection system emitting microwave pulses to measure range and bearing to targets for collision avoidance and navigation in poor visibility.
encyclopedia.content:
A marine radar (Radio Detection and Ranging) is an active electronic navigation system used to detect surface vessels, landmasses, and weather fronts regardless of visibility. Unlike passive receivers or collision-avoidance equipment linked to [how GPS works](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/), radar emits its own electromagnetic pulses and measures the echo delay and angle of arrival to calculate target distance and bearing.

On recreational sailing craft, compact radome antennas operating in the X-band (9.3–9.5 GHz, ~3 cm wavelength) are standard. According to Wikipedia, a sailing mast is a vertical spar designed to carry sails as well as elevated navigational equipment such as radar scanners. The scanner's height above the waterline directly governs the radar horizon; an antenna mounted at 4 meters (13.1 ft) provides a theoretical radar horizon of approximately 4.4 nautical miles (NM) for a surface-level target.

Horizontal beamwidth for standard yacht radomes ranges from 3.5° to 6°, defining the radar's bearing resolution. Skippers must distinguish active radar from passive radar reflectors and AIS broadcasts, which only report cooperative targets. Safe operation requires manual fine-tuning of gain control alongside sea clutter and rain clutter suppression filters to avoid losing small fiberglass or wooden hulls on the display, while keeping heading alignment tied to [a marine compass](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/).
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Refers specifically to active microwave radar systems. Do not confuse with passive radar reflectors or Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders.

encyclopedia.definition: A tall vertical spar or extruded profile erected along the centerline of a vessel to support sails, standing rigging, and navigational hardware.
encyclopedia.content:
A mast is a tall vertical spar erected along the vessel's centerline to support sails, rigging, and equipment. Modern sailing yachts typically utilize extruded aluminum profiles or carbon fiber masts. It is essential to distinguish a sailing mast from land-based utility towers or horizontal spars like the boom. As noted in historical references from Wikipedia, until the mid-19th century all masts were crafted from timber, with larger ships using multi-section built masts to achieve necessary height and structural strength.

The main purpose of the mast is to carry the mainsail and headsails while withstanding severe dynamic forces. Standing rigging (forestay, backstay, and shrouds) holds the mast stable, while spreaders optimize guy angles. Key measurements include mast height above the waterline (air draft, measured in meters or feet), mast rake (angle of tilt in degrees), and cross-sectional wall thickness (in millimeters). Proper mast tuning heavily impacts vessel balance during [essential sailing maneuvers](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/) like tacking and gybing. Additionally, halyards run inside or along the mast profile, requiring precise [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/) to hoist and adjust sails safely. Masts also serve as elevated platforms for radar domes, VHF antennas, and navigation lights.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Measured by air draft (height above waterline) and rake angle. Distinguish from horizontal spars (booms) or non-marine structural poles.

encyclopedia.definition: The international standard radiotelephone distress signal transmitted over VHF/HF radio to indicate grave and imminent danger to a vessel or human life.
encyclopedia.content:
The word "MAYDAY" (derived from the French phrase *m'aider*, meaning "help me") is the primary voice distress signal used in maritime VHF and HF radiotelephony under GMDSS regulations. It holds absolute priority over all other transmissions. A MAYDAY call is initiated by stating "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" on VHF Channel 16 (156.8 MHz). It must be reserved strictly for situations involving grave and imminent danger to a vessel or human life, such as severe uncontained fires, sinking, capsizing, or an urgent order to abandon ship.

Skippers must carefully distinguish MAYDAY from the urgency signal PAN-PAN (used when safety is threatened but no immediate grave danger exists) and the safety signal SECURITE. When extreme weather conditions—monitored via accurate [weather forecast sites](/en/blog/weather-forecast-sites-your-guide-to-the-most-accurate-marine-weather-websites-for-sea-and-sailing/)—cause sudden hull damage or severe flooding, sending a distress message becomes necessary. The standard distress message structure includes: MAYDAY, vessel name, call sign, MMSI number, position, nature of distress, required assistance, and number of persons on board.

Historically, MAYDAY serves as the voice equivalent of the Morse code SOS signal (which Wikipedia notes was established by the 1906 International Radiotelegraph Convention). Once a MAYDAY broadcast is heard, all other marine stations must immediately cease transmitting on Channel 16. Nearby coastal authorities or a local [yacht marina](/en/blog/what-is-a-yacht-marina-port-vs-marina-for-yachts-explained-2/) receiving the call will immediately relay the distress signal to national search and rescue services.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Spoken three times consecutively ("MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY") on VHF Channel 16 (156.8 MHz) or 2182 kHz. Used exclusively when immediate assistance is required.

encyclopedia.definition: A monohull is a vessel featuring a single hull structure, relying on a weighted ballast keel to provide righting moment and transverse stability under sail.
encyclopedia.content:
A monohull is the traditional configuration for sailing and motor vessels, characterized by a single continuous hull structure. Unlike multihulls such as catamarans, a sailing monohull achieves transverse stability through a heavily ballasted keel, which typically accounts for 30% to 45% of the boat's total displacement. As wind fills the sails, the vessel heels over—typically operating at heel angles between 15° and 25°—generating a righting moment that continuously pulls the hull back toward an upright position.

Standard cruising monohulls range in length overall (LOA) from 9 to 20 meters (30 to 65 feet), with a draft generally between 1.5 and 3.2 meters depending on the keel configuration. Mastering sail control on a monohull requires a firm understanding of basic [yachting terminology](/en/blog/yachting-terminology-for-dummies-77-words-you-need-to-know-before-traveling-on-a-yacht/), as well as trimming techniques to manage heel angle and helm balance. When evaluating options, sailors often compare the tight turning circle and sea-kindly motion of a [catamaran or monohull](/en/blog/catamaran-or-monohull-which-to-choose-for-your-next-trip/) for offshore passages.

According to Wikipedia reference data, high-performance monohull design reaches its peak in the IMOCA 60 class (18.3 meters or 60 feet LOA), governed by the International Monohull Open Class Association. Monohulls are uniquely capable of self-righting even after a 180-degree capsize, making them highly resilient for ocean sailing.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Monohull specifically denotes a single-hulled craft, contrasting with catamarans (double hull) and trimarans (triple hull).

encyclopedia.definition: A high-elasticity synthetic rope used to secure a vessel to a quay, pier, mooring buoy, or alongside another vessel.
encyclopedia.content:
A mooring line (also referred to as a mooring warp or berth line) is a heavy-duty, highly elastic rope used to secure a vessel to a quay, pier, mooring buoy, or alongside another boat. According to Wikipedia, a mooring is any permanent structure to which a vessel is secured to forestall its free movement on the water.

Sailors must distinguish mooring lines from other onboard cordage. Unlike running rigging (such as halyards and sheets), which demand low-stretch materials like Dyneema to preserve sail shape, mooring lines require high elasticity. They are typically constructed from three-strand or braided polyamide (nylon) or polyester, capable of 15–25% elongation under stress to absorb shock loads caused by swell and wind gusts. Mooring lines also differ from anchor rodes, tow lines, and heavy commercial hawsers in both construction and handling.

A reliable rule of thumb for sizing is 1 mm of line diameter per 1 m of the boat's length overall (LOA). For a 12-meter (40 ft) sailing yacht, lines with a diameter of 12 to 14 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 2,500 kg are standard. Recommended minimum lengths are 1.5 × LOA for bow and stern lines, and 1.0 to 1.2 × LOA for forward and aft springs.

Properly preparing lines before entering a crowded [yacht marina](/en/blog/what-is-a-yacht-marina-port-vs-marina-for-yachts-explained-2/) ensures safe berthing. Understanding how to handle these lines is a fundamental part of mastering [essential yachting terminology](/en/blog/yachting-terminology-for-dummies-77-words-you-need-to-know-before-traveling-on-a-yacht/) and seamanship.

encyclopedia.definition: A graphic representation of a maritime area and adjacent coastal regions, providing detailed information on water depths, hazards, channels, and aids to navigation.
encyclopedia.content:
A nautical chart is a specialized map designed specifically for marine navigation. Unlike standard land maps (which detail terrestrial topography) or business process charts, a nautical chart focuses on sea features. It accurately represents water depths (soundings in meters, feet, or fathoms where 1 fathom equals 1.8288 meters or 6 feet), seabed composition, coastline features, hazards, and navigational aids like buoys and lighthouses.

Distance on a nautical chart is measured in nautical miles (NM), where 1 NM equals exactly 1,852 meters (or 1 minute of latitude). Charts primarily use Mercator projection, allowing mariners to plot straight-line courses (rhumb lines). Scales vary depending on purpose: harbor charts (1:5,000 to 1:20,000) provide fine detail for confined waters, while coastal and ocean charts (1:100,000 to 1:1,000,000) cover vast sea areas.

In modern seamanship, electronic navigational charts (ENCs) integrated into chartplotters dominate daily use. However, paper charts remain essential backups. Master modern tools alongside traditional skills by learning [how GPS works and the role of electronic navigation](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/). Furthermore, understanding basic map symbols is a fundamental part of mastering [essential yachting terminology](/en/blog/yachting-terminology-for-dummies-77-words-you-need-to-know-before-traveling-on-a-yacht/) before taking command of any vessel.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Essential for passage planning and dead reckoning. Mariners must keep paper and digital charts updated via Notices to Mariners.
encyclopedia.seoTitle: Nautical Chart: Definition, Scale & Marine Navigation
encyclopedia.seoDescription: Learn what a nautical chart is, how depths and scales are measured, and why it is crucial for safe navigation at sea.

encyclopedia.definition: A unit of distance used in marine and air navigation, defined internationally as exactly 1,852 meters.
encyclopedia.content:
The [nautical mile](/en/tags/navigation/) (NM or nmi) is the fundamental unit of distance in maritime and aeronautical navigation. Historically defined as the arc length corresponding to one minute (1/60th of a degree) of latitude along a meridian, it directly ties geographic coordinates to physical distance on sea charts. Today, by international standard adopted in 1929, one international nautical mile is defined as exactly 1,852 meters (approximately 6,076.1 feet or 1.151 statute miles).

Because latitude scales on Mercator projection paper charts represent arc minutes of latitude, sailors can directly measure distances in nautical miles using a pair of dividers against the latitude scale on the side of the chart. One minute of latitude equals one nautical mile.

The derived unit for speed at sea is the knot (kn), defined as one nautical mile per hour. For instance, a yacht sailing at 6 knots covers 6 nautical miles in one hour. Distance calculations in passage planning, fuel consumption, and collision avoidance rely entirely on nautical miles and knots rather than kilometers or land miles. In classical sailor lore, milestones were celebrated through traditions such as swallow tattoos, where each swallow traditionally represented 5,000 nautical miles sailed. In modern navigation, electronic systems like GPS and AIS plot coordinates and calculate distances using nautical miles.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Abbreviated as NM, nmi, or M. Speed in knots equals nautical miles per hour. Do not confuse with statute miles (1,609 m).

encyclopedia.definition: A control line in the running rigging of a sailboat that attaches the mainsail clew to the boom and adjusts the tension along the foot of the sail.
encyclopedia.content: The outhaul is a fundamental sail control line used to shape the mainsail. As defined by Wikipedia, it is an element of the running rigging that attaches the mainsail clew to the boom and tensions the foot of the sail. It typically employs a block at the aft end of the boom and a cleat further forward to secure the line. By tightening the outhaul, the sail's foot is stretched, flattening the lower section of the mainsail and reducing its camber (draft). This is desirable in stronger winds to depower the sail and reduce heeling. Loosening the outhaul allows the foot to become fuller, increasing camber and generating more power in light airs. Proper adjustment is crucial for efficient sail trim. On many cruising yachts, the outhaul is a simple line led to a cleat on the boom, while racing setups may include purchase systems for finer control. For a deeper understanding of how lines like the outhaul interact with other deck hardware, see our guide on [yacht rope handling and winches](/en/blog/rabota-s-verevkami-na-yahte-lebedki-i-bloki-dlya-chaynikov/). Sail designer Frank Bethwaite recommended marking the boom with outhaul settings for different wind speeds, a practice still used by many racers. Explore more about [sail handling and trim](/en/tags/sail-handling-trim/) to master all your sail controls.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Adjust the outhaul before setting sail and fine-tune as wind conditions change. In light winds, ease it for a fuller shape; in heavy winds, tension it to flatten the sail. Always ensure the clew is securely attached to the boom.

encyclopedia.definition: The international radiotelephone urgency signal, broadcast three times ("PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN") on VHF Channel 16 to indicate an urgent situation concerning the safety of a vessel or person without immediate grave danger.
encyclopedia.content:
The international urgency signal "PAN-PAN" derives from the French word *panne* (breakdown) and is utilized in maritime VHF radio communications to signal urgent situations involving the safety of a vessel or individual. Unlike the distress signal MAYDAY, which is reserved for grave and imminent danger threatening human life or the loss of the vessel, PAN-PAN denotes an urgent condition where immediate life-threatening danger is absent. Typical scenarios include engine loss in open waters without an imminent drift toward lee shores, steering failure, or an urgent medical consultation request (PAN-PAN MEDICO).

Under GMDSS standards, the call is transmitted on VHF Channel 16 (frequency 156.8 MHz) at standard high power (25 W). The proper format requires repeating "PAN-PAN" three times, followed by the target addressee, vessel name, call sign, MMSI number, precise position, nature of the urgency, and requested assistance. This nautical terminology must be distinguished from homonyms such as the Pan American Games (Pan Am Games multi-sport event noted in Wikipedia records).

In cases of mechanical malfunction, a skipper might broadcast a PAN-PAN to secure a tow toward a protected [yacht marina](/en/blog/weather-forecast-sites-your-guide-to-the-most-accurate-marine-weather-websites-for-sea-and-sailing/). Monitoring reliable [weather forecast sites](/en/blog/what-is-a-yacht-marina-port-vs-marina-for-yachts-explained-2/) further helps crews anticipate severe conditions before an urgency call becomes necessary.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Transmitted on VHF CH 16 by repeating the words PAN-PAN three times before the message content. Has priority over all routine radio traffic except MAYDAY.

encyclopedia.definition: A nautical term denoting the left side of a vessel when facing forward towards the bow, a sailing vessel's wind orientation (port tack), or a harbor facility.
encyclopedia.content:
In maritime navigation, the term "port" carries three distinct definitions that every sailor must understand. Primarily, port refers to the entire left side of a vessel when facing forward towards the bow. Historically derived from the side facing the port or quay during loading, it replaced the older English term "larboard" to prevent oral misinterpretation with "starboard". To ensure visibility during night operations, the port side displays a red sidelight visible across an exact sector arc of 112.5° (from directly ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam).

Secondly, the term describes a sailboat's point of sail known as "port tack". As noted in Wikipedia, a craft is on a port tack when the wind blows over its port (left) side, with the sails trimmed over to the starboard side. Under Rule 12 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs), a vessel sailing on a port tack must keep clear and give way to a vessel sailing on a starboard tack.

Finally, "port" functions as a noun for a commercial or recreational harbor equipped with maritime facilities. Whether configuring modern [electronic navigation systems](/en/blog/sailing-superstitions-from-neptune-to-the-ban-on-bananas-on-board/) or observing traditional [sailing superstitions](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/), clear communication using standardized nautical terminology remains crucial. Confusing port with starboard during helm commands or collision avoidance maneuvers presents severe safety risks at sea.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Use 'port side' for vessel orientation, 'port tack' for wind direction status under COLREGs Rule 12, and 'port' when referencing harbor facilities or traditional steering commands.

encyclopedia.definition: An underwater hydrodynamic blade forming part of a vessel's steering system, used to control or alter the yacht's heading by deflecting water flow.
encyclopedia.content:
It is essential to distinguish between the helm control (a steering wheel or tiller) and the rudder blade itself—the submerged hydrodynamic profile that generates turning force. The rudder blade connects to the steering mechanism via the rudder stock, a shaft passing through the hull via the stock tube or stuffing box.

When the rudder blade deflects from the centerline, moving water creates asymmetrical pressure across its surfaces, swinging the stern and altering the boat's heading. The maximum effective deflection angle for most sailing rudders is between 30° and 35°. Exceeding this limit causes hydrodynamic stall, drastically increasing drag while reducing turning moment.

Common configurations include spade rudders (unsupported, highly maneuverable) and skeg-hung rudders (supported by a structural fin for added protection). In the event of steering cable failure, an emergency tiller is fitted directly to the head of the rudder stock.

Maintaining the steering system is paramount for offshore safety. As noted in Wikipedia documentation regarding Iberian orca interactions, the rudder is often the primary point of mechanical vulnerability during physical impacts from marine life. When performing basic maneuvering techniques like [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/the-compass-on-a-sailboat-how-to-use-a-marine-compass-and-why-sailors-need-it/), smooth helm application prevents unnecessary drag. Furthermore, keeping a steady course by monitoring your [magnetic compass](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/) ensures minimal rudder correction, optimizing vessel speed and hydrodynamic efficiency.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Do not confuse the rudder blade with the wheel or tiller. Avoid over-steering beyond 35 degrees to prevent loss of turning authority due to hydrodynamic stall.

encyclopedia.definition: A point of sail where a vessel travels in the same direction as the true wind, at an angle of approximately 180° (typically between 170° and 190°).
encyclopedia.content:
Running downwind is a point of sail in which the true wind blows directly or nearly directly from behind the vessel, aligned at approximately 180° (170°–190°) relative to the bow. As described in Wikipedia's overview on points of sail, a sailboat on a run relies primarily on drag rather than aerodynamic lift to generate forward thrust, with the sails acting much like a parachute.

Understanding [courses relative to the wind in yachting](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/) is essential for efficient sail trimming. When running downwind, the mainsail is eased out almost perpendicular to the centerline, while the foresail is often set on the opposite side in a "goose-winged" (or wing-and-wing) configuration, or replaced by a spinnaker. The primary practical hazard of running downwind is an accidental or uncontrolled gybe, caused by sudden wind oscillations or steering errors that force the boom to swing violently across the deck. To mitigate this risk, crews routinely rig a boom preventer. Practitioners must distinguish between "running" as a steady state point of sail and the act of executing a gybe maneuver. Mastering these concepts is fundamental alongside practicing [essential sailing maneuvers for beginners](/en/blog/courses-relative-to-the-wind-in-yachting-a-beginner-s-guide/) to maintain safety while sailing off the wind.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: "Running downwind" (or simply "running") denotes a point of sail. It should not be confused with the maneuver of gybing (jibing), which is the turn during which the stern crosses the wind.

encyclopedia.definition: The bottom edge of a sail, running between the tack and clew.
encyclopedia.content:
The sail foot is the bottom edge of a sail, running between the tack (forward lower corner) and the clew (aft lower corner). According to Wikipedia, sail components include features that define a sail's shape and function, and the foot plays a key role in shaping the sail's aerodynamic profile. On a mainsail, it is typically attached to the boom via a bolt rope or slides, though loose-footed mainsails are also common, where the sail is only fixed at the corners. On a jib, the foot is always free and tensioned through the clew. The foot length is specified in sail dimensions and measured in meters or feet; do not confuse with the imperial unit 'foot' (plural 'feet'). For a mainsail, this measurement is often denoted as 'E' in rig dimensions. The exact length is measured straight-line between the centers of the tack and clew.

Foot tension is adjusted with the outhaul, which stretches the sail along the boom. Increasing tension flattens the sail, reducing draft and power—useful in strong winds. Easing the outhaul adds depth to the profile, increasing drive in light air. For example, in fresh breeze, it's advisable to tension the foot firmly to reduce heeling and maintain control. In light wind, conversely, ease the outhaul to create a fuller shape and more power. Proper adjustment directly affects boat speed and handling. When performing maneuvers like [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/rabota-s-verevkami-na-yahte-lebedki-i-bloki-dlya-chaynikov/), correct foot tension helps maintain control. Working the outhaul often involves winches and blocks; the basics are covered in [Yacht Rope Handling: Winches and Blocks for Beginners](/en/blog/osnovnye-parusnye-manevry-dlya-novichkov-overshtag-i-fordevind-prostymi-slovami/). For a broader look at sail trim, see the [Sail Handling & Trim](/en/tags/sail-handling-trim/) section.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Not to be confused with the imperial unit of length 'foot' (plural 'feet').

encyclopedia.definition: The practice of reducing a sail's active surface area to maintain vessel stability, reduce heel, and preserve control in strong winds.
encyclopedia.content:
Sail reefing is a fundamental sail-handling technique designed to reduce the active surface area of a sail as wind speed increases. The primary objective of reefing is to minimize heel angle, prevent helm overpower, and reduce mechanical stress on the rig and hull. In nautical terminology, the noun "reef" refers to the portion of the sail rolled or folded away, distinguishing it from geological underwater reefs.

Skippers typically initiate reefing when apparent wind speeds reach 15 to 20 knots (Beaufort Force 4 to 5). On a modern sloop, the mainsail is reefed using slab reefing systems—where the halyard is eased and the sail is secured to the boom with reef pennants—or via in-mast and in-boom furling mechanisms. Headsails are commonly shortened using a headsail furler.

Executing a reef efficiently requires coordinated crew work and proper [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/), as releasing the halyard and tensioning the reefing line must be controlled using clutches and winches. Reefing early is essential when encountering sudden squalls or a descending [catabatic wind](/en/blog/what-is-a-catabatic-wind-and-how-is-it-dangerous-for-boaters/), ensuring the boat remains manageable and fast. Returning to full sail area is known as shaking out a reef. As noted in Wikipedia, reefing involves folding or rolling one edge of the canvas to stow the unused sail area against a spar or stay.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Used to maintain vessel stability and balance when wind strength increases. A common rule of thumb is to reef when you first think about it.

encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia, a winch is a mechanical device used to adjust tension on a rope or wire rope. On modern sailing yachts, sheet and halyard winches function as modified capstans: rather than spooling and storing line on the drum, line passes around the drum under friction while the free tail leaves the device.

Sailboat winches are classified by power ratio, such as 40:1 or 46:2, indicating the mechanical advantage provided by internal gear assemblies when turning the winch handle. A two-speed winch provides lower gearing when turning the handle clockwise and higher gearing counter-clockwise. Most modern cruising yachts utilize self-tailing winches featuring a top feeder arm and spring-loaded jaws designed for line diameters typically ranging from 8 mm to 14 mm. This self-tailing mechanism strips the line automatically, eliminating the need for a dedicated crew member to tail while another cranks.

In practical deck operations, proper friction management requires wrapping the line clockwise around the drum—usually 3 to 4 turns depending on load and line material. Using fewer turns risks slippage under high loads, while excessive turns can cause dangerous riding turns. For comprehensive deck safety and handling procedures, refer to [yacht rope work winches and blocks for beginners](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/). Distinguish marine sheet winches from industrial anchor windlasses or drum winches, which physically store cable around an internal spool rather than passing line through under continuous manual or electric control.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Always insert the handle fully until the locking pin clicks. Remove handles when not actively cranking to prevent injury or overboard losses.

encyclopedia.definition: A heavy-weather drag device deployed from the bow of a vessel to hold its head into the wind and waves, significantly reducing downwind drift.
encyclopedia.content:
A sea anchor (or parachute anchor) is a specialized fabric device deployed from a vessel’s bow into open water to create hydrodynamic drag rather than anchoring to the seabed. According to Wikipedia, its primary function is to stabilize the boat in heavy weather and limit drift downwind. By keeping the bow pointed into the wind and breaking seas, it prevents dangerous broadside rolling (broaching) or capsizing.

It is critical to distinguish a sea anchor from a drogue: a sea anchor is large, deployed from the bow, and aims to virtually stop the vessel (reducing drift to 0.5–1.5 knots), whereas a drogue is smaller, trailed behind the stern, and designed to control speed while running downwind.

Proper deployment requires precise dimensions and rigging. The anchor rode length should ideally measure 10 to 15 times the vessel's length overall (LOA), usually combined with a heavy chain leader or weight to keep the line submerged and damp surge loads. A dedicated tripping line attached to the crown of the parachute cone is necessary to collapse the canopy for retrieval. While modern skippers rely heavily on [electronic navigation tools](/en/blog/sailing-superstitions-from-neptune-to-the-ban-on-bananas-on-board/) to monitor leeway, storm seamanship remains anchored in sound practical knowledge passed through centuries of [sailing traditions](/en/blog/how-gps-works-and-the-role-of-electronic-navigation-in-the-world-of-sailing/).
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Rig the sea anchor with a bridle to bow cleats and fit chafing gear to the rode. Never attempt to haul a deployed sea anchor without pulling the tripping line first.

encyclopedia.definition: A running rigging line used to trim a sail by controlling its angle relative to the wind and its tension.
encyclopedia.content:
According to Wikipedia, in sailing, a sheet is a line (rope, cable or chain) used to control the movable corner(s) (clews) of a sail. In practical yachting, sheets are essential running rigging components that control sail trim, shape, and angle of attack relative to the apparent wind. Unlike halyards, which hoist sails vertically, sheets control horizontal position and leech tension. The primary types are the mainsheet (attached to the main boom or clew) and jib or genoa sheets (attached to the foresail clew).

On modern sailing yachts between 30 and 50 feet in length, sheets are constructed from low-stretch braided polyester or Dyneema core ropes with diameters typically ranging from 8 to 14 mm. Proper line diameter balances tensile strength, friction in blocks, and hand comfort. During maneuvers such as [tacking and gybing](/en/blog/yacht-rope-work-winches-and-blocks-for-beginners/), sheets are eased and trimmed continuously. Safe execution relies on correct [yacht rope handling](/en/blog/essential-sailing-maneuvers-for-beginners-tacking-and-gybing-in-simple-terms/) around winches and sheet stoppers.

In English terminology, it is vital to distinguish the nautical noun "sheet" from homonyms such as bed sheets, sheet metal, or paper sheets. In seamanship, a sheet is strictly a control line, never a sail itself. Accurate sheet trim prevents sail stalling and optimizes aerodynamic drive.
encyclopedia.usageNotes: Standard nautical commands are "trim the sheet" (pull in) and "ease the sheet" (let out).
